lectures.title: Sending Signals to Multiple Processes: the `killall` Command

cues.en: In this lecture.
We want to have a look at the kill all command.
The kill All command.
We can also use that one for sending signals.
But the difference to kill is that we can select the process by name.
This is already built in.
We don't need to do anything here with our bash.
So, for example, kill all Firefox would get all processes with the name Firefox and then kill them
if we have a look at that.
So for example, here we can see Firefox is open right now and I could now for example, just kill that
one with the kill all command, kill all Firefox and we can see Firefox has been killed.
The next thing is that we can also use kill all to send other signals to processes.
So for example, we could also use it to send a Sigint by using kill all minus S and then the signal
and then the name of the process.
So we can check that one as well.
So for example here kill all minus S in Firefox and we can see now we have sent a Sigint signal and
the reason or the the result is the same Firefox is closed.
Now, however, if you are running on Mac minus S has a different meaning, it will make the program
more talkative and it will prevent any signals from being sent.
So for example, if I go to my Mac here and I would say kill all minus s sig in Firefox, in that case,
minus S is a standalone parameter.
So it will just make us or it will make the kill all program.
Just print the kill commands it wants to send instead of executing them.
And this is then just here for decoration in a sense.
So this one now does nothing here.
So on Mac, we need to use the other way to write it.
We can only use the following syntax here by using a dash in front of the signal that we want to send.
And this will then also work on Mac.
This this way of writing It would also work on Linux.
But I do I personally do prefer to use minus S and then the name of the signal.
But let's have a look at whether this works.
So here for example, kill all minus Sig and Firefox and now Firefox has been closed.
So it was on a different monitor, so you probably can't see it, but we can see it has worked and the
second time we try to execute it, we get a message that it could not find any processes to kill.
So you can see here how this kill all program allows you to more easily find processes by name and then
to send a signal to them.
